topic: classifying quadrilaterals from defining properties (high-school geometry)
subtitle: Naming the most specific quadrilateral from the marks on a figure, classifying from what the diagonals do, and classifying from vertex coordinates

problems.note: Both pairs of opposite sides marked parallel forces a parallelogram; opposite angles are congruent, so 5x = 75.
No congruence or parallel marks at all: nothing beyond the 360 degree interior-angle sum is available.
Four congruent sides plus one right angle forces a square; adjacent sides are equal, so 3x - 5 = x + 7.
Diagonals bisect each other AND are congruent forces a rectangle; congruent diagonals give 4x - 6 = x + 9.
Back-substitute to report the common diagonal length AC.
Four congruent sides with perpendicular bisecting diagonals forces a rhombus; the right angle at the centre puts the two marked angles in one triangle.
Slope of side AB for A(-2,1), B(2,3), C(4,-1), D(0,-3).
Slope of the adjacent side BC; the product with AB's slope is -1, so the angle at B is right.
Length AB, rounded to two decimal places.
Length BC equals AB, so the rectangle is in fact a square.

problems.desc: Always/sometimes/never with justification: is a rhombus a rectangle? The student must name the defining property that separates the two families and mark on the given rhombus what would have to be added. Open reasoning - manual review.

Proof-style classification argument: one pair of opposite sides both congruent and parallel forces a parallelogram; the student must argue it and then decide whether a rectangle is forced. Open written proof - manual review.
